claims.claim: Codex core is a stateful local runtime that mediates model proposals rather than being the model itself.

evidence.point: Repository overview assigns reusable model/tool/conversation logic to codex-core.
Session owns configuration, model client, operations, events, tools, and persistence hooks.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Some execution and integrations live in sibling crates or external services; local does not mean single-process.
claims.final_wording: Codex is not the model; it is a stateful runtime that mediates model output and coordinates local or delegated capabilities.

claims.claim: TUI, app-server, IDE, and MCP surfaces adapt user input and runtime events around shared core behavior.

evidence.point: Crate map separates core from tui, app-server, protocol, and MCP crates.
App-server processors translate requests into core thread/turn operations and notifications.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Surfaces can contain surface-specific workflows and are not mechanically identical adapters.
claims.final_wording: The surfaces share core engine behavior while adding their own transport and presentation logic.

claims.claim: A model request is a structured projection of retained history plus current instructions, environment facts, and visible tool specifications.
claims.target_location: docs/architecture/01-system-overview.md Context assembly; 03-threads-turns-persistence.md Context is a projection; diagram 06

evidence.point: Turn construction builds a prompt and model-visible tools from current turn/session state.
History, normalization, compaction, and truncation construct the retained model input.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Exact fragments and ordering vary by feature, provider, and task type.
claims.final_wording: Model input is a curated projection of retained history and current runtime facts, not arbitrary process state.

claims.claim: A normal user turn can contain repeated model samples separated by tool execution and correlated tool outputs.

evidence.point: The turn loop samples, handles response items/tools, and continues sampling with outputs.
Registry converts handler results to model-visible response input items.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: A turn can finish without a tool call, fail, be cancelled, or enter a specialized task flow.
claims.final_wording: A normal turn may repeat model → tool → correlated output → model until it finishes or terminates another way.

claims.claim: The runtime carries the model call ID through routing and returns it on the function/custom-tool output.

evidence.point: ToolCall/ToolInvocation and output conversion retain call_id.
Router tests assert the resulting output shape for routed calls.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Transport-specific tools may use additional identifiers, but the model-call correlation remains.
claims.final_wording: A routed function/custom-tool result is returned with the originating model call ID.

claims.claim: A registered tool runtime and a tool specification visible to the current model are not necessarily the same set.
claims.target_location: docs/architecture/02-agent-tool-loop.md Route and validate; 07-formal-operational-model.md Derived functions and Tool-call lifecycle

evidence.point: spec_plan builds runtimes/registry and separately computes model_visible_specs.
Specification tests cover tools hidden or selected by mode/features.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Normal providers are expected to emit calls from supplied specifications; this does not imply hidden calls are routinely observed.
claims.final_wording: Registration proves a handler exists; exposure records whether its schema was advertised for that model request.

claims.claim: The generic tool registry does not enforce model exposure as a dispatch-time authorization check.

evidence.point: Registry dispatch looks up a registered runtime and parses payload; exposure is computed separately in spec_plan.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: A provider or concrete handler can reject a call for other reasons; negative source search is bounded to the inspected generic path.
claims.final_wording: Exposure should normally hold for model-originated calls, but making it a security invariant requires an explicit check or equivalent guarantee beyond generic registry lookup.

claims.claim: Local command execution policy distinguishes skip approval, needs approval, and forbidden outcomes.

evidence.point: ExecApprovalRequirement contains Skip, NeedsApproval, and Forbidden paths derived from policy decisions.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Reasons, amendments, and retry behavior make the real enum richer than the guide's three labels.
claims.final_wording: For governed command paths, policy can skip approval, request it, or forbid execution, with additional reason/amendment detail.

claims.claim: User approval and local process sandboxing are separate controls.

evidence.point: Approval is an awaited session/client decision.
Sandbox policy/command construction remains a separate execution step.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Exact enforcement varies by OS and execution backend.
claims.final_wording: For local command/patch paths, approval decides whether to attempt an action and the sandbox separately constrains the resulting process.

claims.claim: The local process sandbox does not automatically constrain external MCP servers, connectors, or cloud services.
claims.target_location: docs/architecture/02-agent-tool-loop.md Permission; 06-trace-a-turn.md Side effects; 07 formal model

evidence.point: Inspected OS sandbox construction is attached to local shell/patch execution.
MCP is a separate transport/server interface with its own requests and implementation wiring.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Some remote environments may implement their own sandbox; that is a different enforcement boundary.
claims.final_wording: Remote tool families require explicit authorization and isolation at their own credential, process, and service boundaries.

claims.claim: Every completed tool call has exactly one correlated terminal result in all reachable runtime states.

evidence.point: Normalization supplies missing outputs and removes orphan outputs, establishing coherent pairing for model history.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: The inspected normalizer did not establish a repository-wide proof that duplicate matching outputs can never exist.

claims.claim: Normalized model history supplies an output for retained tool calls that need one and removes orphan outputs.
claims.target_location: docs/architecture/02-agent-tool-loop.md Why normalization matters; 07 formal model Correlation after normalization

evidence.point: normalize.rs pairs calls/outputs, inserts aborted output for missing cases, and removes orphan outputs.
Tests cover missing-call and missing-output transcript cases.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: This is scoped to normalized model history, not every raw durable record.
claims.final_wording: A tool call retained in normalized model history has a correlated output; orphan outputs are removed and missing outputs are represented as aborted.

claims.claim: Turn interruption signals cooperative cancellation to active work rather than relying only on UI state.

evidence.point: Session/task state owns cancellation tokens and interrupt handling.
Tool invocation/orchestration carries cancellation and cleanup behavior.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: A concrete tool can require cleanup or fail to stop immediately; cancellation is not instantaneous process annihilation.
claims.final_wording: Interrupting a turn marks runtime cancellation and signals active tools; completion can require handler-specific cleanup.

claims.claim: Rollout storage is an immutable append-only event log.
claims.target_location: docs/architecture/README.md former rollout definition; 03 persistence former append-only wording

evidence.point: Recorder appends JSONL but can repair/truncate an interrupted tail, update metadata, and add compacted/materialized records.
Tests exercise append/flush and tail-repair behavior.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Append-oriented is accurate; immutable append-only is too strong.
claims.final_wording: Rollout is append-oriented reconstruction history with explicit tail repair and derived compaction/metadata behavior.

claims.claim: Resume constructs a new live session from recorded thread/rollout state rather than reviving old in-memory task objects.

evidence.point: Thread manager reads/reconstructs history and creates a session for start/resume/fork.
V2 tests exercise resume/fork lifecycle across requests.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Loaded session caches and ephemeral sessions change which storage backend participates.
claims.final_wording: Resume reconstructs usable history into a new live session; it does not revive the previous process's cancellation token or running task.

claims.claim: Every runtime event and external side effect is durably persisted.
claims.target_location: docs/architecture/02-agent-tool-loop.md former results list; 06 trace former events-to-rollout wording

evidence.point: Session has distinct event emission and rollout recording paths.
Recorder persists selected rollout items rather than proving capture of every external effect.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Live deltas and service-side effects need not have one-to-one durable records.
claims.final_wording: Selected response and lifecycle items are recorded according to persistence policy; event streams and durable records overlap but are not identical.

claims.claim: The ordinary user-turn path gives a live session one active normal task at a time.
claims.target_location: docs/architecture/03-threads-turns-persistence.md Turn; 07 formal model serialization rule; diagram 04

evidence.point: Session active-task ownership serializes normal submitted work and handles replacement/cancellation.
Historical protocol describes at most one task, consistent with the central model but not authoritative.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Specialized review/compaction task kinds and internal parallel tools make an unqualified 'only one task' claim too broad.
claims.final_wording: A live session serializes the ordinary user-turn model loop while permitting controlled internal parallelism and specialized task flows.

claims.claim: Context compaction and tool-output truncation are mechanisms used to keep admitted model input within applicable limits.
claims.target_location: docs/architecture/03-threads-turns-persistence.md Context; 07 formal model Context and safety property 4; diagram 06

evidence.point: Compaction and truncation paths respond to history/tool-output pressure and model limits.
Contributor rule requires model context to remain structured and bounded.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: No unconditional proof says every attempted input can be compacted successfully; visible failure remains possible.
claims.final_wording: An admitted request should obey its active size policy; compaction/truncation pursue that postcondition and can fail rather than guarantee all input fits.

claims.claim: Live events and durable reconstruction records are distinct representations with different consumers.
claims.target_location: docs/architecture/03-threads-turns-persistence.md; 06-trace-a-turn.md Events versus durable records; 07 formal tuple H versus E

evidence.point: Core separately emits Event values and invokes rollout persistence paths.
Recorder stores rollout items for reconstruction independent of live subscribers.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: The same action can produce both, and some event/item types are closely related.
claims.final_wording: Events drive connected clients; recorded rollout/thread items support history and reconstruction. They overlap but are not interchangeable.

claims.claim: App-server is a JSON-RPC adapter/connection manager around core thread and turn operations, not a separate model/tool loop.

evidence.point: Message processors route versioned requests to core thread/session operations and map resulting events.
Protocol crate defines client requests, notifications, and server requests separately from core implementation.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: App-server owns substantial connection, subscription, configuration, and surface-specific behavior.
claims.final_wording: App-server translates versioned JSON-RPC lifecycle and connection concerns around shared core engine behavior.

claims.claim: Each app-server connection must perform initialize followed by initialized before ordinary requests are accepted.
claims.target_location: codex-rs/app-server/README.md Lifecycle overview and Initialization; docs/architecture/04 and diagram 05

evidence.point: README specifies initialize-once and initialized acknowledgement ordering.
Initialize processor and connection state reject not-initialized and repeated initialize cases.
Connection tests cover handshake errors and success.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: In-process embedding still uses equivalent connection state even when transport differs.
claims.final_wording: An app-server connection performs initialize/initialized before normal method use; invalid ordering is rejected.

claims.claim: App-server uses bounded internal queues and can return overload errors rather than buffer without limit.

evidence.point: README states ingress, processing, and outbound queues are bounded and documents overload behavior.
Message processing uses bounded channel/overload paths.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Exact capacity and timing behavior are implementation/configuration details.
claims.final_wording: App-server applies bounded queueing and exposes overload instead of promising unlimited buffering.

claims.claim: The v2 app-server lifecycle is organized around threads, turns, and streamed items/notifications.
claims.target_location: codex-rs/app-server/README.md Threads and Turns; docs/architecture/03 and 04

evidence.point: V2 protocol declares thread/start/read/list/resume/fork, turn/start/interrupt, item types, and notifications.
V2 suites exercise these lifecycle methods.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Experimental methods extend this model and legacy v1 names remain for compatibility.
claims.final_wording: V2 clients create/read/resume/fork threads, start or interrupt turns, and consume item/turn notifications.

claims.claim: App-server approval is bidirectional: the server can request a decision and correlate the client's response.

evidence.point: Protocol separates ClientRequest, ServerRequest, and responses including approval methods.
Approval integration tests exercise request/response round trips.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Not every tool family uses the same approval method.
claims.final_wording: App-server supports correlated server-to-client approval requests and client decisions.

claims.claim: Experimental app-server methods require explicit capability opt-in where designated and are not stable production contracts.

evidence.point: README labels transports/methods experimental and documents capabilities.experimentalApi.
Protocol method metadata distinguishes experimental APIs.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Not all APIs in the document are experimental; stability must be checked method by method.
claims.final_wording: Treat designated experimental methods and transports as opt-in and unstable; check each method's status rather than generalizing to all v2 APIs.

claims.claim: Checked-in app-server protocol types and generated schemas are the authoritative source for exact wire shapes at the pinned commit.

evidence.point: Schema-generation section points to protocol definitions/workflow.
Versioned Rust types and schema artifacts enumerate wire fields and methods.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Runtime processors establish behavioral semantics; types alone do not prove successful execution.
claims.final_wording: Use the versioned protocol types/generated schemas for exact shapes and the processors/tests for behavior.

claims.claim: The app-server websocket transport is experimental and unsupported for production workloads.

evidence.point: Transport section explicitly labels websocket experimental/unsupported and warns against production reliance.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: This is a declared support status, not a claim that websocket code never works.
claims.final_wording: Websocket transport exists but is explicitly experimental and unsupported for production reliance.

claims.claim: The experimental process/spawn app-server API starts a host process without the Codex sandbox.

evidence.point: Method description explicitly says process/spawn runs without the Codex sandbox.
Experimental process method types are declared in the protocol.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Host OS/account controls still apply; 'without Codex sandbox' does not mean without all constraints.
claims.final_wording: Experimental process/spawn bypasses the Codex sandbox and therefore has a distinct, higher-risk host-process boundary.

claims.claim: protocol_v1.md is a current authoritative specification of core behavior.

evidence.point: The document itself warns that code might not completely match and says submissions are primarily in-process types rather than a stable wire contract.
Current external API types live in versioned app-server protocol modules.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: It remains useful for terminology and explicit v1 serialization compatibility notes.
claims.final_wording: Read protocol_v1.md as historical/conceptual documentation and verify current behavior in code and versioned protocol types.

claims.claim: The core conceptual interface uses submissions into Codex and events back to the driving UI, historically described as SQ/EQ.
claims.target_location: codex-rs/docs/protocol_v1.md Entities and Interface; docs/architecture/04 Core protocol

evidence.point: Document defines Submission Queue and Event Queue and maps Op/EventMsg directions.
Current session exposes submit/next_event style operation and event flow.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Concrete transports and app-server JSON-RPC do not literally expose the same queue pair.
claims.final_wording: SQ/EQ is a useful historical conceptual model for core submissions and events, not a universal external wire transport.

claims.claim: V1 turn-start and turn-complete events retain task_started/task_complete serialization compatibility.

evidence.point: Compatibility note specifies serialized task_* tags and accepted task_*/turn_* deserialization.
Checked-in protocol types provide the current compatibility representation.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Scoped to v1 serialization, not v2 method names.
claims.final_wording: V1 compatibility retains task_started/task_complete wire tags for turn lifecycle events.

claims.claim: The Codex MCP server control interface is experimental and subject to change without notice.

evidence.point: Title, status block, and closing note explicitly mark the interface experimental and unstable.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: This refers to Codex-as-MCP-server control interface, not the stability of the MCP standard generally.
claims.final_wording: Treat the Codex MCP control interface as experimental and verify names/shapes against current protocol code.

claims.claim: The experimental Codex MCP control interface exposes v2 thread/turn methods, typed notifications, and approval round trips over MCP transport.
claims.target_location: codex-rs/docs/codex_mcp_interface.md Overview, v2 API, approvals; docs/architecture/04

evidence.point: Document enumerates v2 methods, notifications, and server-request approvals.
Underlying v2 method and message types exist in the shared protocol definitions.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Experimental status means the mapping can evolve and server wiring must be checked for implemented coverage.
claims.final_wording: At the pinned commit, the experimental MCP control surface maps core v2 thread/turn lifecycle, notifications, and approvals onto MCP transport.

claims.claim: Codex uses different local sandbox mechanisms and compatibility paths on macOS, Linux, and Windows.
claims.target_location: codex-rs/core/README.md platform sections; docs/architecture/01 sandbox component

evidence.point: Support matrix describes Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap/Landlock paths on Linux, and Windows elevated/restricted-token backends.
Sandbox selection produces platform/backend-specific execution policy.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Exact capability depends on platform version, helper availability, policy representability, and selected backend.
claims.final_wording: Local sandbox enforcement is platform/backend-specific; do not infer identical behavior from a shared high-level policy name.

claims.claim: Unsupported split-filesystem policies are always silently weakened on Windows.

evidence.point: README states policies requiring unsupported carveouts/reopened descendants fail closed rather than run with weaker enforcement.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Some policies can round-trip to legacy behavior and remain supported.
claims.final_wording: Windows accepts policies its selected backend can enforce or represent without semantic loss; specified unsupported cases fail closed.

claims.claim: The architecture guide is a machine-checked formal verification of Codex.

evidence.point: Primary TLA+ material distinguishes actual formal specifications/checking from an informal state-machine explanation.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: The page uses mathematical notation but contains no TLA+ module, proof, or model-checker result.
claims.final_wording: The page is an engineering model mixing pinned observations and labeled normative properties; it is not machine-checked verification.

claims.claim: The guide's symbols are standard elementary set/predicate/state-transition notation and are defined locally for non-specialists.

evidence.point: MIT material provides primary instructional background for predicates and sets.
Lamport material provides state-machine/temporal-specification background.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Eventually is explicitly informal here and the page is not complete TLA+ syntax.
claims.final_wording: Read the formulas as locally defined engineering shorthand; use the linked primary teaching resources for deeper set, predicate, and state-machine background.

claims.claim: If all external dependencies respond, every non-cancelled turn is proven eventually to advance, block visibly, or complete.

evidence.point: Session code contains progress, wait, cancellation, and completion paths but no fairness proof.
Formal liveness requires temporal assumptions/fairness beyond an informal transition sketch.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Scheduler fairness, handler termination, transport loss, retries, and unmodeled failures prevent this pass from proving liveness.
claims.final_wording: Conditional progress is a desired design hypothesis; no deadline, scheduler fairness, or liveness proof is claimed.

claims.claim: A pending command/patch approval prevents that governed local side effect from starting until a decision resolves the waiter.
claims.target_location: docs/architecture/07-formal-operational-model.md approval transition and safety property 3; diagram 03

evidence.point: Approval request helpers emit/request a decision and await the response.
NeedsApproval path precedes shell/patch execution and denial produces a non-executed outcome.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Scoped to concrete governed operations; it does not assert every external tool uses this waiter.
claims.final_wording: For command/patch paths using the session approval flow, pending approval is a real execution pause.

claims.claim: Every side effect in the current repository goes through one universal policy and sandbox layer.

evidence.point: Strong explicit policy/sandbox flow exists for local commands/patches.
Remote MCP capabilities cross a separate server/transport boundary.
Experimental process/spawn explicitly runs without Codex sandbox.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Tool families have heterogeneous boundaries; a universal current-repository claim is false in scope even though explicit controls are good design advice.
claims.final_wording: For a system you build, require every side-effecting tool family to name and test its actual authorization and isolation boundary.

claims.claim: Separating durable/recovery history from the model-context projection is a supported design pattern in Codex.

evidence.point: Context manager derives normalized/compacted input from retained history.
Recorder stores reconstruction-oriented rollout records separately from an individual sampling request.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Retention/redaction policy determines whether stored history is a complete audit trail.
claims.final_wording: Keep reconstruction/audit records conceptually separate from the smaller projection sent to the model, with explicit retention policy for both.

claims.claim: The six Mermaid diagrams accurately summarize component ownership, the normal tool loop, local approval/sandbox gates, thread reconstruction, app-server handshake, and context projection after the wording corrections in this pass.

evidence.point: Supports session, event, approval, and persistence relationships.
Supports routing/registry/tool-loop relationships.
Supports start/resume/fork reconstruction.
Supports app-server handshake and request/event flow.
Supports normalization/compaction projection.

claims.counterevidence_or_limits: Diagrams intentionally omit error branches, specialized tasks, handler-specific remote authorization, and most protocol fields.
claims.final_wording: Treat the diagrams as scoped high-level paths with the stated omissions, not exhaustive control-flow graphs.
